reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder with a complete absence of functional fibrinogen, caused by mutations in FGA, FGB, or FGG
Bleeding often begins in the neonatal period, classically as umbilical stump haemorrhage
All clot-based coagulation tests are grossly abnormal (prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and thrombin time) because fibrin cannot form
Fibrinogen activity and antigen are unmeasurable, distinguishing afibrinogenaemia from hypo- and dysfibrinogenaemia where some fibrinogen is present
Paradoxically, both bleeding and thrombosis can occur, and spontaneous splenic rupture is a recognised complication
Recurrent miscarriage and placental abruption reflect the requirement for fibrinogen in maintaining pregnancy
Management uses fibrinogen concentrate replacement for bleeding, procedures, and pregnancy, with prophylaxis in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrinogen is the soluble plasma protein that thrombin converts to fibrin, the structural scaffold of the clot, and it also supports platelet aggregation by bridging activated platelets. Congenital afibrinogenaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in one of the three fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, FGG), abolishing production or secretion of the protein. Without fibrinogen, no fibrin clot can form and platelet aggregation is impaired, so all fibrin-dependent coagulation assays are markedly prolonged and haemostasis fails, producing bleeding that frequently manifests at birth. The same molecule is required for placental integrity, so its absence causes recurrent pregnancy loss and abruption. A coexisting thrombotic tendency reflects loss of fibrinogen's normal role in binding and clearing thrombin, leaving unbound thrombin free to act elsewhere.
additionalDifferentials: Other severe inherited coagulation factor deficiencies
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with fibrinogen consumption
Severe liver disease with impaired fibrinogen synthesis
Vitamin K deficiency or anticoagulant effect
additionalInvestigations: Fibrinogen activity (Clauss) assay, which is unmeasurable
Fibrinogen antigen assay to confirm absence of protein
Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and thrombin time, all markedly prolonged
Reptilase time as a confirmatory fibrin-formation test
Genetic testing of FGA, FGB, and FGG
Imaging for suspected intracranial or intra-abdominal (including splenic) haemorrhage
redFlags: Intracranial haemorrhage or other major spontaneous bleeding
Spontaneous splenic rupture or intra-abdominal haemorrhage
Thrombotic events, which can occur despite the bleeding phenotype
Pregnancy complications including recurrent miscarriage and placental abruption
reference.prognosis: With fibrinogen concentrate replacement, bleeding episodes can be controlled and pregnancies supported, giving a reasonable outlook, though patients face lifelong risks of both haemorrhage and thrombosis requiring specialist management.
pitfalls: Confusing afibrinogenaemia with dysfibrinogenaemia by relying on a single test rather than both activity and antigen
Forgetting that these patients can thrombose as well as bleed
Overlooking fibrinogen replacement to sustain pregnancy
Attributing grossly abnormal clotting times to DIC or liver disease without measuring fibrinogen
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
